# Step 1 — Forest Fire Point Extraction: Audit & Documentation

**Folder:** `Forest fire Extraction in INDIA(2000-2022)/`
**Notebook:** `FOREST_FIRE_POINTS_EXTRACTION(INDIA).ipynb` (generated by `build_notebook.py`)
**Outputs:** `Forest_Fire_Outputs/`
**Audit date:** 2026-08-22 (read-only; no code executed, no notebook edited)

---

## What Was Done

Step 1 builds this project's fire-point ground truth: it takes the raw MODIS Collection
6.1 FIRMS archive for the India region (`fire_archive_M-C61_772720.csv`, **2,804,373**
raw detections, 2000–2022) and reduces it to **541,545 real forest-fire points**
through a documented, executed sequence of filters:

| Stage | Rows remaining | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Raw MODIS archive | 2,804,373 | 0 dropped for invalid date/lat/lon |
| After India bbox pre-filter | 2,801,347 | cheap rectangle pre-filter (68–97.5°E, 6.5–37.5°N) |
| After exact India polygon clip | 1,599,471 | **1,201,876 points excluded** — detections inside the bbox but outside India's real border |
| After study-period clip (2000-11-01–2022-12-15) | 1,599,471 | no additional loss (archive already period-scoped) |
| After exact-duplicate removal | 1,599,466 | 5 exact `(lon, lat, date)` duplicates dropped |
| After forest-LULC pixel filter (per-year) | **541,545** | ~33.9% of all-India fire points fall on forest land cover |

Forest cover, computed from the same yearly ESA-CCI/C3S rasters used for filtering,
holds at **9.86–10.43%** of India's land area across the 23 study years (`extraction_summary.csv`).
Peak year is 2021 (111,467 total / 38,116 forest fire points); the low is 2000
(1,419 / 225 — a partial year, study period starts 2000-11-01).

All 27 available LULC years (1992–1995, 2000–2022) came from real extracted ESA-CCI/C3S
ZIPs (31 ZIP files scanned); the notebook's own log shows `Missing years: []` for the
2000–2022 study span, i.e. **no nearest-year LULC fallback was actually needed** for any
study year, even though the code path exists for that case.

Six summary plots plus a boundary plot were generated and saved to
`Forest_Fire_Outputs/plots/`, and a separate supplementary analysis (added later, not
part of the same notebook — see Completeness Audit) validates the fire-point archive
against MODIS MCD64A1.061 burned area (Pearson r=0.915, p<0.0001, n=23 years) and against
Biswas et al.'s own published annual counts (this project runs 0.5–2.4% higher across all
20 overlapping years, 2001–2020).

## How It Was Done

- **Data**: MODIS Collection 6.1 FIRMS CSV (per-detection fields include `latitude`,
  `longitude`, `acq_date`, `confidence`, `type`, `satellite`, `frp`, `bright_t31`, etc. —
  all columns are preserved through to the final output CSV, not dropped).
- **Boundary clip**: two-stage — a cheap lon/lat bbox pre-filter, then an *exact*
  point-in-polygon test (`shapely.contains_xy`) against India's dissolved state
  boundary (`India_State_Boundary.shp`, 37 parts → 1 polygon). The executed run shows
  this second stage is not cosmetic: it removes **1,201,876 points (42.9% of the
  bbox-passing set)** that lie inside the rectangle but outside India's real border
  (Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh, Myanmar, southern Pakistan).
- **Forest filtering**: per study year, the matching ESA-CCI/C3S LULC NetCDF is loaded,
  a binary forest mask is built from the Sannigrahi et al. (2018) forest class codes
  `{50,60,61,62,70,71,72,80,81,82,90,100,110}` (cited to Biswas et al. 2025, p.4863),
  and every fire point is mapped to its exact LULC grid cell via affine arithmetic
  (`row = round((lat - lat0)/dlat)`, `col = round((lon - lon0)/dlon)`) rather than a
  nearest-neighbor spatial join — exact for ESA-CCI's regular grid and GPU-portable.
- **Compute**: the mask build and pixel lookup (the actual bottleneck — a ~124M-pixel
  grid × up to 300k points/year × 23 years) run on GPU via CuPy, with an automatic
  NumPy fallback. The executed run used an NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (34.2 GB VRAM).
  CSV I/O/date parsing stay on CPU/pandas since CuPy lacks string/datetime support.
- **Outputs**: annual CSVs (`forest_fire_points/forest_fire_<year>.csv`), monthly CSVs
  (`monthly_records/<year>/forest_fire_<year>_<mm>.csv`), one combined CSV, an
  `extraction_summary.csv`, and six plots (annual counts, forest-fire % trend, monthly
  distribution, year×month heatmap, spatial hexbin density map, fire-count-vs-forest-cover
  dual axis).

## Why It Was Done This Way

- **Boundary polygon, not bbox** — a rectangular bbox over India's extent also covers
  parts of five neighboring countries with high fire activity; the executed numbers
  (42.9% of bbox-passing points excluded by the polygon) confirm this was not a
  theoretical concern but a large, real source of contamination that a simpler pipeline
  would have silently retained.
- **India_State_Boundary over India_Country_Boundary** — the country file has ~60
  degenerate sliver polygons near the Palk Strait that don't change point-in-polygon
  results but corrupt plot outlines; the state file dissolves cleanly.
- **Forest-LULC filtering by exact affine pixel lookup, not nearest-neighbor spatial
  join** — mathematically exact for ESA-CCI's regular lat/lon grid, and (unlike a
  geopandas/shapely spatial join) trivially vectorizable on GPU, which matters given the
  ~124M-pixel × hundreds-of-thousands-of-points-per-year scale.
- **One extraction method, not two** — an earlier version of this notebook carried both
  the affine-lookup method and an unexecuted vector/spatial-join path; the latter was
  dropped because it duplicated logic without adding correctness and doesn't port to GPU.
- **Study period capped at 2022-12-15** — ESA-CCI/C3S LULC data (needed for every year's
  forest mask) doesn't exist beyond 2022, so extending the fire archive further would
  produce unfiltered, non-forest-validated points — a correctness choice, not a
  convenience one.

## Impact on Spatial Fire Mapping in India

Step 1 is the only step in the pipeline that produces an *independent, real* ground-truth
label set — every other step (NDVI, LST, FLDAS, terrain/accessibility) produces
*predictor* features that later get joined against these 541,545 points (or their
gridded presence/absence derivative) for supervised training. Concretely:

- It is the sole source of the binary fire/no-fire signal Step 6/7's Random Forest and
  Step 8's PINN models are trained and evaluated against — model AUC numbers reported
  downstream are only as trustworthy as this step's spatial and temporal fidelity.
- The exact-boundary clip directly protects spatial-mapping validity: without it, a
  meaningful fraction of "Indian" fire risk would actually reflect Sri Lankan, Nepali, or
  Bangladeshi fire regimes with different vegetation, climate, and land-management
  drivers — a genuine confound for any spatial susceptibility map produced downstream.
  Excluding 1.2M non-Indian points at this stage is what keeps every later spatial
  product (density maps, susceptibility rasters) actually about India.
  A national forest-cover estimate consistent to within ~0.6 percentage points
  (9.86–10.43%) across 23 independently-processed years is a useful internal-consistency
  check that the same forest definition is being applied year over year, which matters
  because Step 6 later reuses this same forest-class definition for its LULC
  forest-fraction feature.
- Because points are geolocated to sub-pixel MODIS precision and forest-filtered per
  calendar year (not a single static forest mask), the resulting map correctly reflects
  real land-cover change (e.g. rising forest-fire-point share in high-deforestation or
  reforestation years) rather than freezing India's forest extent at one snapshot.

## Comparison with Biswas et al. (2025)

Biswas et al. build their MaxEnt susceptibility model on **presence-background**
sampling — presence points from a fire dataset, background points sampled from the
study area at large — rather than deriving a full, independently-validated fire-point
archive of their own; MCD64A1.061 burned area appears in their paper as a separate
dataset (their Table 2), not as one of the 15 Table 3 predictors, and not as a
cross-validation check on their presence data.

This project instead performs true point extraction: every one of the 541,545 forest-fire
points is an individual MODIS-detected fire event, geolocated, dated, and forest-filtered
against the land-cover state of that specific year — then, uniquely, cross-validated two
ways that Biswas et al. do not perform for their own presence data: (1) correlated against
an independent product (MCD64A1.061 burned area, r=0.915) and (2) checked year-by-year
against Biswas et al.'s own published annual counts, where this project runs consistently
0.5–2.4% higher (mean +1.0%) across all 20 overlapping years — a small, explainable,
non-random offset that itself functions as external validation of this project's
extraction methodology against theirs. Where this project is weaker is exactly the
disclosed gap below: Biswas et al.'s presence-background approach is not exposed to
FIRMS's own per-detection confidence/type quality flags either, but neither project
currently performs the confidence filtering or spatial declustering that is now standard
practice in the wildfire-modeling literature for point-process fire data (see below).

## Completeness Audit: Gaps Found

1. **No FIRMS confidence-level filtering or spatial thinning/declustering** — already
   known and disclosed by the project. Confirmed still present in the executed pipeline:
   `confidence` and `type` columns are read and preserved through to
   `all_forest_fires_2000_2022.csv` but never used as a filter. In the final 541,545
   points, 23,236 (4.29%) have `confidence < 30` (a commonly used "low confidence"
   threshold in FIRMS-based studies). **Priority: high (deferred by design)** — this is
   the pipeline's ground-truth label set, so any change here cascades to every downstream
   step; the project has explicitly and reasonably chosen to defer it rather than
   destabilize already-trained downstream models.

2. **`type` field (MODIS "presumed vegetation fire" vs. "other static land source" /
   "offshore" / "volcano") is also never filtered** — a related but distinct gap from
   #1. In the final output, 1,122 points (0.21%) carry `type=2` ("other static land
   source") and 2 carry `type=3` ("offshore"); negligible in volume but a free,
   near-zero-cost filter (`type == 0`) that isn't applied. **Priority: low** (tiny
   volume, but trivial to add whenever confidence filtering is eventually tackled).

3. **The burned-area validation analysis (`Monthly_BurnedArea_MCD64A1.csv`,
   `Annual_BurnedArea_vs_FireCount.csv`, `Biswas2025_AnnualFireCount_Comparison.csv`,
   `plots/BurnedArea_vs_FireCount.png`) exists only as committed output artifacts** — the
   script/notebook that produced them is not present anywhere in this repo or in
   `build_notebook.py`; only the git commit messages (`bde1f85`, `992b5d7`, `3760403`)
   describe what was done. **Priority: medium** — a genuine reproducibility gap for a
   Q1 submission: a reviewer or co-author cannot currently re-run this specific analysis
   from the tracked codebase, only inspect its outputs.

4. **No diagnostic plot for confidence-level distribution** — despite the field being
   loaded and retained, there is no histogram/plot showing the confidence distribution of
   retained points (which would visually justify, or motivate, the deferred filtering in
   #1). **Priority: low-medium** — cheap to add, doesn't touch the label set, and would
   strengthen the "known gap, consciously deferred" narrative with a supporting figure.

5. **No land-cover-*class* breakdown of retained points** — the existing plots (02, 06)
   show binary forest-vs-total fire counts and forest-cover % only; there is no
   breakdown of which of the 13 Sannigrahi forest sub-classes (e.g. closed vs. open
   evergreen/deciduous, mosaic classes) the 541,545 points actually fall on. **Priority:
   low** — nice-to-have for a methods figure, not required for the current binary
   forest/non-forest use case, and the 22-class breakdown already exists one step later
   (Step 4/FLDAS land cover).

6. **No sensitivity check on the boundary-polygon choice** — the state-vs-country
   boundary decision is well-justified qualitatively (sliver polygons near the Palk
   Strait), but there is no quantitative check of how many fire points, if any, fall in
   the disputed/sliver zone and would flip in/out under the alternate boundary.
   **Priority: low** — the stated rationale (slivers are near-zero-area and near a
   fire-inactive strait) makes this unlikely to matter, but a one-line sensitivity note
   would remove any reviewer doubt cheaply.

7. **What already exists and is solid, stated plainly**: the six core summary plots
   (annual counts, %-trend, monthly distribution, year×month heatmap, spatial density
   hexbin map, fire-count-vs-forest-cover) cover the standard temporal and spatial
   diagnostics expected for this kind of dataset description, the burned-area
   cross-validation (r=0.915) is a genuine, non-trivial independent check most papers at
   this stage skip entirely, and the year-by-year comparison against Biswas et al.'s own
   published counts is a real, quantified external-validity check on the extraction
   methodology itself — not just on the final risk model. These do not need further work.
